solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Corporation installing computers in a reflective metal

indicators.note: a reflection shows things back to front, so the letters of 'in a' are turned round
to install something is to fit it inside, so the tummy takes the other letters in

parts.note: a corporation is an old jokey word for a paunch, a tum
information technology
IN A, reflected to read ANI

explanation.surface: A company fitting out its computers inside a shiny metal casing.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Corporation’ reads as a business, but it is the old slang for a large belly. The tum opens after its T to take IT and the mirrored IN A.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain definition: titanium is a strong, light, silvery metallic element.

clue.text: Dependency on me fails to work

indicators.note: letters set to work are put into action and rearranged into something useful

parts.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: Someone lamenting that another's reliance on them isn't working out.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Dependency’ looks like emotional reliance, the start of a personal complaint, but it is the political sense: the Isle of Man is a Crown dependency, a self-governing island in the Irish Sea under the British Crown.
explanation.definitionFit: The Isle of Man is not part of the UK but a Crown dependency, so it is literally a dependency.

clue.text: Nemesis of Rachel almost destroyed

indicators.note: almost the whole word, so the last letter is dropped
something destroyed is broken up, so its letters are scattered and reassembled

parts.note: used as is
RACHEL without its last letter

explanation.surface: Someone whose worst enemy was Rachel, who has nearly been wiped out.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Of’ looks like a joining word between definition and wordplay, but its letters are part of the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: A nemesis is a person's principal enemy, their arch-foe.

clue.text: American's reaction to smart Scotsman's clothing

indicators.note: clothing wraps round a body, so the Scotsman's name goes round the cry

parts.note: Ian is a typically Scottish first name
what you say when something smarts, or stings

explanation.surface: An American commenting on a well-dressed Scotsman's outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Smart’ reads as well dressed, which fits the clothing picture, but it is the verb: a sting that makes you say OW. The first ’s stands for ‘is’.
explanation.definitionFit: An Iowan comes from Iowa, a state in the Midwest, so is an American.

clue.text: What you should call surgeon hiding a blemish

indicators.note: to hide something is to keep it inside, so the title holds the A

parts.note: in Britain surgeons are addressed as Mr, not Dr
used as is

explanation.surface: Advice on how to address a surgeon who is covering up a scar.
explanation.walkthrough: A British custom: a surgeon, once qualified, drops ‘Doctor’ and goes back to Mr, Ms or Mrs. Here the verb sense of ‘blemish’ is meant: to mar is to spoil.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the verb sense: to spoil the look of something.

clue.text: Shop U-turning about craftsman

indicators.note: a U-turn sends you back the way you came, so the letters of 'about' run backwards

parts.note: the Co-op, a British chain of shops
RE means about; turned round it reads ER

explanation.surface: A shop doing an about-turn on the craftsman it employs.
explanation.walkthrough: The Co-op is a long-established British cooperative that runs grocery stores.
explanation.definitionFit: A cooper is a craftsman who makes and repairs barrels and casks.

clue.text: Real ale fans drinking last of Singapore sling and avoiding shots?

indicators.note: what you drink goes inside you, so the campaigners take in the letter
take the final letter of the word that follows

parts.note: CAMRA is the Campaign for Real Ale, a British consumer group for traditional beer
the final letter of SingaporE
to shy is to throw or sling, as at a coconut shy

explanation.surface: Beer lovers sipping a cocktail and ducking any shots of spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: A Singapore sling is a gin cocktail, so ‘sling’ looks welded to Singapore; it is a separate verb meaning throw. ‘Shots’ in the definition are photographs, not drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone camera-shy avoids having photographs, or shots, taken; the question mark flags the pun on drinks.

clue.text: Blunder due, without international language being recalled

indicators.note: without means lacking here, so the letter is taken away

parts.note: due is OWING; take away I for international

indicators.note: something recalled is called back, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: Lao is the language of Laos; reversed it reads OAL

explanation.surface: A slip in an exam, with an international language being called to mind.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Due’ is owing, as money is owed. An own goal in football is one a player accidentally scores against their own side.
explanation.definitionFit: An own goal is figuratively any blunder that harms your own cause.

clue.text: Force out European citizen without reserve

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the reserve's letters come off the citizen

parts.note: the standard abbreviation
a citizen is a SUBJECT; take away SUB, a reserve player

explanation.surface: A demand to deport a European national with no hesitation.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Without reserve’ reads as ‘unreservedly’, but the reserve is a substitute, SUB, removed from SUBJECT.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to throw someone out, as from a club or a pilot's seat.

clue.text: Section of Jenga almost lands together

indicators.note: almost the whole word, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: a Jenga tower is built of wooden blocks; BLOCK loses its last letter

explanation.surface: A player's Jenga piece nearly lands, holding the tower together.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Lands’ looks like a verb for something falling, but it is the noun: countries.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloc is a group of countries allied together, as in the Eastern bloc.

clue.text: Grandiloquent writer to come back around, claiming genius but lacking English

indicators.note: turned around, so the word runs backwards
lacking means without, so the E is removed
to claim something is to take hold of it, so the reversed word surrounds the genius

parts.note: hair or plants that regrow come back; turned round it reads WORGER
a genius at something is a DEMON; take away E for English

explanation.surface: A pompous author making a comeback, claiming genius but having no grasp of English.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Come back’ looks like a return to form, but it is regrowing, turned round. A demon, as in a demon at chess, is someone brilliant at something.
explanation.definitionFit: A wordmonger is a writer who uses words showily or for effect, fairly called grandiloquent.

clue.text: One might like 16's tail more elegant

parts.note: to tail someone is to follow them, to dog them
fancier means more elaborate or elegant

explanation.surface: A tale about which dog has the smarter tail.
explanation.walkthrough: 16 across is SALUKI, a hound, so the one who likes it is a dog lover. ‘16’s tail’ looks like the saluki's tail, but ’s is ‘is’ and ‘tail’ is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog fancier is an enthusiast for dogs, so might well like a saluki.

clue.text: Fashionable? That's what was said about gold tooth

parts.note: what's fashionable is in

indicators.note: about as in turned about, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: sic is inserted in a quotation to mean ‘that is what was written’; turned about it reads CIS
or is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: A question about fashion, and gossip about someone's gold tooth.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘About gold’ looks like a topic, but ‘about’ turns SIC round, and gold comes after it.
explanation.definitionFit: An incisor is one of the narrow cutting teeth at the front of the mouth.

clue.text: Court may require this number eight seed?

parts.note: an oat is a cereal grain, a seed
H is the eighth letter of the alphabet

explanation.surface: A tennis court needing its number eight seed.
explanation.walkthrough: The seeds of a tennis tournament are ranked, so ‘number eight seed’ sounds like a player; it is H after OAT. The seed comes first in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A witness in a law court is required to swear an oath before giving evidence.

clue.text: I don't recall debut of Michael Caine as staggering

definitions.note: the definition is what the answer would say; an amnesiac is a person who does not recall

indicators.note: letters that stagger lurch about, so they are rearranged
a debut is a first appearance, so take the first letter

parts.note: the first letter of Michael
anagram fodder

explanation.surface: An actor who can't remember seeing Michael Caine's astonishing first film.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Staggering’ reads as ‘amazing’, praise for Caine's debut, but it is the anagram instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: ‘I don’t recall’ is exactly what an amnesiac, someone who has lost their memory, would say.

clue.text: Where spoon goes for it?

definitions.meaning: literally, the place a spoon is dipped at a meal
informal British for ‘in trouble’, as in ‘you’re for it now’

explanation.surface: A question about where you put your spoon.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one riddle about cutlery, but ‘for it’ is a separate idiom meaning in trouble, and the question mark flags the literal reading.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom both ways: to be in the soup and to be for it both mean facing trouble, and the soup is also literally where the spoon goes.

clue.text: Hound backers out of traditional part of Boxing Day party

indicators.note: the backers of a word are its back letters, and each one is taken out

parts.note: Boxing Day, 26 December, is when British shops hold their SALE; drop the E
UKIP, the UK Independence Party; drop the P

explanation.surface: Hounding the supporters out of a festive party.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Backers’ reads as political supporters of the party, but it means the back letters of both words. Boxing Day is the British holiday on 26 December.
explanation.definitionFit: A saluki is a tall, slender hunting hound from the Middle East.

clue.text: Like to look up Ken Loach movie souvenirs

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means read from the bottom, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: as means like
to peek is to look
Kes is Ken Loach's 1969 film about a boy and his kestrel

explanation.surface: A fan looking up Ken Loach films and collecting mementoes of them.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue ‘up’ reverses what comes before it, so both halves of the first part are turned round together, and only then is the film tacked on.
explanation.definitionFit: Keepsakes are small things kept in memory of someone or something, souvenirs.

clue.text: Slight help for diabetics dropping in time

indicators.note: to drop something is to let it go, so IN leaves the word

parts.note: INSULIN with IN removed
the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A small help for diabetics arriving just in time.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Dropping in’ looks like visiting, but it tells you to drop the letters IN.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the noun sense: a snub or affront.

clue.text: Someone who's got fresh bread item from bakery under courier

indicators.note: in a down clue, what is under something sits below it

parts.note: UPS is a parcel delivery company
a tart is a baked pastry; in a down clue it sits under UPS

explanation.surface: A baker's customer who has just picked up a loaf and a pastry from the courier.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Fresh bread’ belongs with the bakery picture, but ‘bread’ is slang for money: the upstart has new money. So the definition runs further than it seems.
explanation.definitionFit: An upstart has risen suddenly to wealth or position, someone with freshly acquired bread, or money.

clue.text: Who falls for fun truant keeping you distracted at first

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so the truant holds the letters

parts.note: a skiver, in British slang, is someone who dodges school or work

indicators.note: take the first letter of each word

parts.note: the first letters of You Distracted

explanation.surface: A truant who has you so distracted you fall for his fun.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Falls for’ suggests being taken in, but it is literal: a skydiver falls out of a plane for pleasure.
explanation.definitionFit: A skydiver is someone who jumps from aircraft and free-falls for sport.

clue.text: Didn't acknowledge or deign to move

indicators.note: letters made to move change places

parts.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

explanation.surface: Someone who refused to acknowledge another or even deign to budge.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Deign’ sits so naturally beside ‘acknowledge’ that it passes as part of the picture rather than fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To ignore someone is to fail to acknowledge them.

clue.text: Accessories for jumper's neck when cycling

indicators.note: cycled letters go round, so the last one comes to the front

parts.note: to neck is British slang for to kiss; move the last S to the front

explanation.surface: Accessories to wear on a jumper's neck when out on a bike.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Jumper’ is British for a sweater, and a neck and accessories fit it perfectly; here it is a ski jumper, and ’s means ‘is’.
explanation.definitionFit: Skis are the equipment a ski jumper wears.

clue.text: Quite nice answer

parts.note: nice means kind
the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A lukewarm reply: the answer was quite nice.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Quite nice’ reads as one phrase, but ‘quite’ is the whole definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Kinda, informal for ‘kind of’, means quite or somewhat.

clue.text: A writ's seen to alter who's heard in court?

indicators.note: to alter something is to change it, so the letters change order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

explanation.surface: A lawyer's writ being redrafted to change which witness is heard in court.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Heard in court’ reads as ‘called to give evidence’, but it also describes someone who heard what happened. The question mark flags the double reading.
explanation.definitionFit: An earwitness testifies to what they heard, and is also someone heard in court.

clue.text: Is resident of 2 perhaps shown up without carbon fibre?

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means read upwards, so the word runs backwards
without means lacking, so C is removed

parts.note: used as is

parts.words: resident of 2 perhaps shown up without carbon
parts.note: a Manx person is a CELT, perhaps; reversed it reads TLEC, then lose C for carbon

explanation.surface: A question whether someone from the Isle of Man has been exposed as lacking carbon fibre.
explanation.walkthrough: 2 down is ISLE OF MAN, whose people count among the Celts; ‘perhaps’ marks that as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Istle is a strong fibre from Mexican agave and yucca plants, used for cord and brushes.

clue.text: I oppose Erdogan tag on Istanbul cops

definitions.note: the definition is what the answer would say; an antagonist is a person who opposes

indicators.note: to cop something is to catch hold of it, so the phrase holds the answer

parts.note: erdogAN TAG ON ISTanbul

explanation.surface: A protester opposing an electronic tag that Istanbul police put on Erdogan.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Cops’ looks like the police of Istanbul, but it is the verb: the phrase cops, or catches, the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: ‘I oppose’ is the motto of an antagonist, one who actively opposes another.

clue.text: Current representative for Sprite

parts.note: I is the symbol for electric current
a Member of Parliament represents a constituency

explanation.surface: A current spokesman for a lemon-lime soft drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Sprite is a fizzy drink brand, which pulls ‘current representative’ towards advertising; the capital hides the small mischievous spirit.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a small mischievous spirit of folklore.

clue.text: Carefully examine Playboy?

definitions.meaning: the verb sense: to search through thoroughly, as with a garden tool combing the ground
a dissolute man of fashion, as in Hogarth's Progress

explanation.surface: An instruction to scrutinise an issue of Playboy magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: Playboy with a capital looks like the magazine, but it is the dissolute man.
explanation.definitionFit: To rake is to search or scan carefully, and a rake is a pleasure-seeking libertine.

clue.text: Hollywood location scout finally getting report about portable tech

parts.note: Hollywood is in Los Angeles

indicators.note: one thing about another goes round it

parts.note: a report is a bang, a pop

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so only the scout's last letter is used

parts.note: the last letter of scouT

explanation.surface: A film location scout at last filing a report on a portable gadget.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Report’ looks like a written account, which suits a scout, but it is a loud noise.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a portable computer that rests on the lap.

clue.text: Pretentious to add Brussels sprouts?

parts.note: a postscript, PS, is something added to a letter
Brussels is the seat of the European Union
sprouts are a dish, by way of example

explanation.surface: A snob thinking it affected to add Brussels sprouts to the menu.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Brussels sprouts’ is a single vegetable, but it splits: Brussels stands for the EU, and sprouts are an example of a dish.
explanation.definitionFit: Pseudish, from the British slang pseud, means pretentious or affected.
